title: Characters and quotients of split diagonalizable groups over rings
statement: Let $A$ be a nonzero commutative ring, $S=\operatorname{Spec}A$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum], and $M,N$ finitely generated abelian groups. Write $D_A(M)=\operatorname{Spec}A[M]$ with the Hopf operations of [def-sfb-ring-diagonalizable-group]. Every $S$-group homomorphism $D_A(M)\to D_A(N)$ is, on a Zariski open cover of $S$, uniquely of the form $D_A(u)$ for a homomorphism $u:N\to M$, with Hopf map $e_n\mapsto e_{u(n)}$; the corresponding $u$ is locally constant on $S$. Such a homomorphism is a closed immersion [def-weil-closed-immersion] exactly when these local $u$ are surjective. For a fixed $u$, its kernel is $D_A(\operatorname{coker}u)$ and its fppf sheaf image is $D_A(\operatorname{im}u)$, embedded in $D_A(N)$ by $N\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{im}u$. In particular, if $L\subseteq M$ is an additive subgroup, the fppf sheaf quotient of $D_A(M)$ by $D_A(M/L)$ is $D_A(L)$; the quotient map is faithfully flat and finitely presented. Fppf sheaf image and quotient are the sheafifications of the pointwise image and quotient for faithfully flat finitely presented coverings. All displayed kernel, image and quotient descriptions commute with arbitrary base change. Two homomorphisms between these split diagonalizable groups that agree on every geometric fibre are equal. These assertions include torsion in $M,N$, and nonreduced $A$.

source.place: Conrad, Appendix B.1, opening discussion and Remark B.1.2, printed pp.280--281; character antiequivalence and quotients of diagonalizable groups; used explicitly in Theorem 5.1.8, printed p.140. Read online; WANTED locally as literature/conrad-reductive-group-schemes.pdf. No Stacks tag states this relative structural theorem.

proof.text: Translate an $S$-morphism into its $A$-algebra map $\varphi:A[N]\to A[M]$ by the natural affine adjunction. The affine product is the spectrum of the tensor product. The tensor-product universal property gives $A[M]\otimes_AA[M]\cong A[M\oplus M]$: send $e_m\otimes e_{m'}$ to $e_{(m,m')}$; the inverse sends the basis symbol back to that tensor. The inverse formulas hold by bilinearity on finite sums. Thus the group and identity diagrams say exactly $\Delta\varphi=(\varphi\otimes\varphi)\Delta$ and $\epsilon\varphi=\epsilon$. Conversely these equations and compatibility with the antipode give a group homomorphism. For the maps $e_n\mapsto e_{u(n)}$, all three Hopf operations commute directly with this formula.

source.place: Lemma 12.4, Remark 12.6 and Theorem 12.9(a),(b), printed pp.232-234; agent extension to arbitrary rings, retaining orthogonal idempotents, and explicit fppf-local proof.

proof.text: If $z=\sum_m c_me_m$ is group-like, comparison of the coefficients of $e_{(m,m')}$ in $\Delta z=z\otimes z$ gives $c_m^2=c_m$ and $c_mc_{m'}=0$ for $m\ne m'$; the counit gives $\sum_mc_m=1$. Conversely these equations give both group-like identities. The nonzero coefficients therefore give a finite partition of $S$ by clopen sets $D(c_m)$; on $D(c_m)$, $z=e_m$. This comparison uses the free finite-sum definition and the tensor basis just constructed, so no domain or reducedness hypothesis enters. The clopen-idempotent lemma supplies both the clopen interpretation and uniqueness of the idempotent belonging to each such open.

source.place: Lemma 12.4, Remark 12.6 and Theorem 12.9(a),(b), printed pp.232-234; agent extension to arbitrary rings, retaining orthogonal idempotents, and explicit fppf-local proof.

proof.text: Apply the preceding calculation to $\varphi(e_{n_i})$ for a finite set of group generators $n_1,\ldots,n_t$ of $N$. Their finitely many partitions have a common finite refinement: its idempotents are the products of one coefficient from each partition. Discard zero products. On each remaining piece $\operatorname{Spec}A_c$, with $A_c=A/(1-c)$ nonzero, every generator maps to one basis vector $e_{m_i}$. Every relation $\sum a_in_i=0$ then gives $e_{\sum a_im_i}=e_0$, hence $\sum a_im_i=0$ by uniqueness of coefficients over the nonzero ring $A_c$. Thus $n_i\mapsto m_i$ determines a unique $u:N\to M$. Equality on the generators proves $\varphi(e_n)=e_{u(n)}$ for every $n$. Empty generators mean the unique map from $N=0$. The assignments agree on nonempty overlaps by the same basis comparison; they give a locally constant $u$.

source.place: Lemma 12.4, Remark 12.6 and Theorem 12.9(a),(b), printed pp.232-234; agent extension to arbitrary rings, retaining orthogonal idempotents, and explicit fppf-local proof.

proof.text: On each nonempty piece of that partition, the image of $A_c[N]\to A_c[M]$ is exactly the $A_c$-span of the basis vectors indexed by $\operatorname{im}u$. This equals $A_c[M]$ if and only if $u$ is surjective: a missing basis vector has coefficient zero in every image. The affine-cover criterion for closed immersions applied to the opens $D_{A_c}(N)$ therefore proves the claimed criterion globally. The nonzero pieces are essential for the converse; they were ensured in the preceding step.

source.place: Lemma 12.4, Remark 12.6 and Theorem 12.9(a),(b), printed pp.232-234; agent extension to arbitrary rings, retaining orthogonal idempotents, and explicit fppf-local proof.

proof.text: For any $A$-algebra $B$, an $A$-algebra map $A[M]\to B$ is exactly a group homomorphism $M\to B^\times$: take the values on $e_m$; conversely extend $e_m\mapsto x(m)$ by finite sums. Thus the kernel of $D_A(u)$ on every test algebra consists of characters $x$ trivial on $\operatorname{im}u$. Such $x$ factor uniquely through $M/\operatorname{im}u$, by $[m]\mapsto x(m)$. This identifies the scheme-theoretic kernel with $D_A(\operatorname{coker}u)$, with its specified inclusion. Indeed the kernel is the fibre product with the identity section; the affine tensor-pushout formula and its universal property represent precisely these test-algebra solutions. This also proves that for every $L\subseteq M$, the map $q:D_A(M)\to D_A(L)$ has kernel $D_A(M/L)$, embedded by $M\twoheadrightarrow M/L$.

source.place: Lemma 12.4, Remark 12.6 and Theorem 12.9(a),(b), printed pp.232-234; agent extension to arbitrary rings, retaining orthogonal idempotents, and explicit fppf-local proof.

proof.text: The subgroup-algebra lemma applies to $L\subseteq M$, since the quotient of the finitely generated group $M$ is finitely generated. It makes $A[M]$ a free $A[L]$-module with nonempty coset basis and gives an explicit finite algebra presentation. Tensoring an $A[L]$-module with this free module is the direct sum of one copy of that module per coset: $v\otimes e_{t_c}\mapsto v$ in coordinate $c$, with inverse given by the same formula backwards. Kernels and images of a direct sum of maps are computed coordinate by coordinate (each element has finite support); a nonempty direct sum of a complex is exact exactly when that complex is exact. Hence this ring map is faithfully flat by the stated definition. It follows that $q$ is flat by the affine flatness criterion and surjective by the faithfully-flat spectrum lemma. The finite presentation gives local finite presentation directly from its definition. Both schemes are affine, hence qcqs; permanence then gives that $q$ is of finite presentation. It is consequently a singleton fppf cover.

source.place: Lemma 12.4, Remark 12.6 and Theorem 12.9(a),(b), printed pp.232-234; agent extension to arbitrary rings, retaining orthogonal idempotents, and explicit fppf-local proof.

proof.text: All the representable functors here are fppf sheaves: an fppf covering is fpqc, and the representable descent lemma gives existence and uniqueness of glued morphisms. For $H=D_A(M/L)$ and $Q=D_A(L)$, the presheaf $P(T)=D_A(M)(T)/H(T)$ maps injectively to $Q(T)$: two lifts have the same image exactly when their ratio lies in the kernel computed above. Every $T\to Q$ lifts after the fppf cover $T\times_QD_A(M)\to T$ obtained by base changing $q$. The local-bijection sheafification lemma therefore identifies $P^\#$ with $Q$. These maps are homomorphisms and the inverse respects products since this holds after the covering lifts; the same uniqueness of sheaf gluing proves it globally. This proves the asserted quotient, rather than asserting that pointwise quotients are already representable.

source.place: Lemma 12.4, Remark 12.6 and Theorem 12.9(a),(b), printed pp.232-234; agent extension to arbitrary rings, retaining orthogonal idempotents, and explicit fppf-local proof.

proof.text: For fixed $u:N\to M$, put $I=\operatorname{im}u\subseteq M$. Factor $u$ as $N\twoheadrightarrow I\hookrightarrow M$. Step 4 makes $D_A(I)\to D_A(N)$ a closed immersion, while Step 6 makes $D_A(M)\to D_A(I)$ an fppf cover; that proof only requires that $M/I$ be finitely generated. On every test scheme the pointwise image presheaf in $D_A(N)$ is a subpresheaf of $D_A(I)$, and every section of $D_A(I)$ belongs to it locally by the base-changed cover. The local-bijection criterion identifies its sheafification with $D_A(I)$. The same factorization with $u$ the inclusion $L\to M$ recovers Step 7. All maps are the stated monomial maps, so these are canonical identifications.

source.place: Lemma 12.4, Remark 12.6 and Theorem 12.9(a),(b), printed pp.232-234; agent extension to arbitrary rings, retaining orthogonal idempotents, and explicit fppf-local proof.

proof.text: For $A\to B$, the tensor-product universal property identifies $B\otimes_AA[M]$ with $B[M]$ by $b\otimes e_m\mapsto be_m$, inverse $\sum b_me_m\mapsto\sum b_m\otimes e_m$. It sends each monomial map, counit and coproduct to the identically indexed one over $B$. The affine fibre-product formula therefore identifies base changes of all the displayed groups and maps with the same constructions over $B$. Steps 5--8 apply over $B$ as well (for $B=0$ all schemes are empty), proving compatibility for kernels, sheaf images and quotients even for nonflat base change. For a general scheme over $S$, apply this on affine opens and glue the explicit monomial identifications. Finally, if two homomorphisms agree on every geometric fibre, refine the two clopen partitions from Step 3 together. Choose a point of a nonempty piece and an algebraic closure of its residue field; the geometric-point description gives a geometric point over it. Equality on that fibre gives equality of all basis indices $u(n_i)$, so the two maps on that piece are the same. Scheme-morphism gluing gives equality globally. Torsion creates no extra basis relations, and nilpotents do not affect the idempotent comparison.
